messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Rivas had been a 40-year-old surgeon in a busy American hospital when the hurricane came through the coastal city where he and his wife were visiting his parents. He had always been the one people turned to in a crisis, but that night he was simply a son and husband caught in a blackout, listening to the wind rip siding from the house and the distant crack of transformers. The evacuation order had come late. In the confusion, a neighboring home caught fire after a generator failed, and the sharp smell of smoke drifted over the block while emergency sirens and metal bangs from collapsing debris cut through the dark. Daniel still described that moment in fragments: the orange light in the rain, his mother crying in the hallway, his own hands trying to pull his family toward the door, and then a strange blankness where other details should have been. Even now he felt as if he remembered only pieces of the event, with whole stretches missing, and when he tried to reconstruct it he was flooded by a grief so intense it felt physical, as if he were back in the ruined street losing people he loved. After the memory had surfaced, ordinary things around him seemed to acquire the same warning quality; a kettle whistling in the break room or a door slamming in the ward could feel like the first sign that something was about to go wrong, and he found himself bracing before he had even identified the sound. He also said that the memory could seize him without warning; a smell in the air or a sudden sound could bring the entire scene back before he had time to brace himself.

In the months that followed, Daniel found himself scanning for danger in ways that surprised him. A loud bang in the operating room, a dropped tray, even a delivery cart striking the wall could make his chest tighten and his thoughts jump back to the hurricane night. The smell of smoke from a neighbor’s grill, or any burnt smell in the hospital cafeteria after someone overheated food, could stop him cold and pull him straight into the memory of the fire nearby. When those cues hit, he would try to outrun them by distracting himself with charts, extra cases, late-night television, anything that could keep his attention pinned elsewhere. At home, he increasingly drank in the evening, telling himself a few drinks took the edge off, and he turned to sexual fantasies and activities as a private way to release the tension he could not otherwise settle. For a while, these habits seemed to help him get through the night, but they also made the memories feel more jagged when they returned: when he was drinking or half-distracted, the fragments came back sharper and less organized, and the incomplete quality of the recollection left him even more convinced that something terrible had been left unfinished or ungrieved.

As the weeks passed, Daniel began to live as if loud noises and smoke were always waiting around the corner. In the hospital he chose the least noisy corridors, stepped out of rooms when alarms blared, and became preoccupied with sniffing the air for anything burnt. At home he avoided the kitchen when something scorched in the oven and found excuses not to attend neighborhood barbecues, because the smell of smoke could bring on the same wave of panic and grief that had once arrived without warning. The more he tried to keep himself busy, drink, or disappear into private relief, the more ordinary moments seemed vulnerable to being pierced by the memory. A single burnt smell on a surgeon’s gown after a case could undo an entire morning; a sharp clang from the unit could make his mind flash back to the storm-dark hallway and the firelight. Daniel had begun to feel that his body was living in anticipation of the next cue, and that his own attempts to blunt the tension were leaving him less anchored, more porous to the memory when it came. He noticed that after nights of drinking or staying up with fantasies, the next day he was more on edge, quicker to interpret a sound as danger, and quicker still to be pulled into that partial, grief-soaked recollection.

By the time he sought help, his marriage had grown quieter and more strained, not because of open conflict but because he was absent even when present, retreating into work, alcohol, and private coping rather than staying with his wife in the evenings. He came to treatment after a particularly brutal week in the operating room, when a cautery odor and an alarm from an adjacent bay had sent him straight back into the hurricane memory and left him shaken for the rest of the day. He was embarrassed that as a surgeon he could be unsettled by noises and smells that other people seemed to tolerate, and he was frightened by how quickly the memory could still overtake him, with missing pieces, sudden grief, and the feeling that he had never fully left that night. What brought him in was the sense that his ways of coping were no longer containing the problem; they were keeping him cycling between tension, brief relief, and a more fragile return of the same memory. What he hoped for was simple but urgent: to stop being ambushed by the smell of smoke, the sting of burnt air, and sudden loud noises, and to reclaim enough steadiness that he could be fully present again with his wife, his work, and his own life.
